summary: Defines part of the Management Information Base for managing the security protocols of Fibre Channel, called FC-SP. It describes managed objects that a network management system can read to monitor information related to FC-SP. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: This is a dashboard layout for a device. It lists the security gauges a manager can read on a storage network, so they can check on things from afar.

questions: how is fibre channel security managed with snmp
subtitle: Five SNMP MIB modules that let a network manager monitor and configure the security features of Fibre Channel storage networks.

tldr.problem: Fibre Channel has its own security protocols (FC-SP) for authentication, key setup, frame protection and fabric policy, but network management systems had no standard SNMP way to see or control them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5324 defines five MIB modules, one for shared types and algorithm identifiers, and one each for authentication, zoning, policy and security associations, plus notifications for key events.
tldr.outcome: A management station can read FC-SP state and change some parameters using ordinary SNMP, though the RFC warns that writable objects need SNMPv3 protection.

today: RFC 5324 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2008. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the definition of these five FC-SP MIB modules.

sections.title: What This MIB Covers
sections.content:
RFC 5324 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for the Fibre Channel Security Protocols, known as FC-SP. FC-SP is specified elsewhere (in the T11 standard the RFC cites as [FC-SP]) and includes protocols to authenticate Fibre Channel entities, protocols to set up session keys, protocols to negotiate parameters for frame-by-frame integrity and confidentiality, and protocols to establish and distribute policies across a Fabric.

The memo was initially developed by the INCITS T11 committee, which approved it for forwarding to the IETF. It follows the Internet-Standard Management Framework: objects are accessed through SNMP and written in SMIv2, as described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580. The RFC itself defines no new protocol on the wire, only managed objects.
sections.eli5: FC-SP is the set of security rules for a storage network. This document does not make new rules. It just makes a standard list of things a manager can look at to see how those rules are going.

sections.title: Fibre Channel Background
sections.content:
Fibre Channel (FC) is logically a bidirectional point-to-point serial data channel built for high performance, and a general transport for higher-level protocols such as SCSI command sets and IP. Communicating points are called N_Ports, joined either by a switching network called a Fabric or by a point-to-point link. A Fabric port a node attaches to is an F_Port, and a switch port joined to another switch by an Inter-Switch Link is an E_Port.

Many FC components have globally unique names, typically formatted as World Wide Names (WWNs). Frames carry 24-bit address identifiers for source and destination, and on a Fabric these addresses are assigned dynamically by a Switch.

Zoning groups devices so that communication is only possible between members of a common zone. Hard zoning is enforced in the Fabric by the Switches, while soft zoning relies on endpoints not sending traffic to addresses they did not get from the Name Server. Virtual Fabrics tag each frame to say which of several Virtual Fabrics it travels on.
sections.eli5: A Fabric is like a big building of connected rooms for computers and disks. Zones are like clubs: you can only talk to people in the same club.

sections.title: Authentication and Security Associations in FC-SP
sections.content:
Two entities may negotiate whether authentication is required and which protocol to use, in switch-to-switch, node-to-switch and node-to-node communication. The protocols perform mutual authentication with optional shared key establishment, and the key can then be used to set up Security Associations. Three kinds of credential are accommodated: secrets (DH-CHAP, which may also use an external RADIUS, Diameter or TACACS server), certificates (FCAP, using a trusted Certificate Authority) and passwords (FCPAP). A fourth protocol, IKEv2-AUTH, uses a Security Association Management transaction to authenticate as well.

The Security Association Management protocol is a subset of IKEv2 (RFC 4306) suited to Fibre Channel, described in RFC 4595. The RFC stresses that it is not IPsec. Traffic Selectors say which traffic is protected by which SA. ESP_Header protects FC-2 frames and CT_Authentication protects CT_IUs. Each entity keeps a Security Association Database holding active SAs, each with an SPI and sequence number counter plus the chosen transforms, and ordered Traffic Selector entries for ingress and egress. SAs are unidirectional but always exist as a pair, one per direction.
sections.eli5: Before two devices trust each other they show proof of who they are, like a password, a secret handshake or an official ID card. After that they agree on a private code for the messages they send next.

sections.title: Fabric Policy Objects
sections.content:
FC-SP adopts two approaches to policy. One is a Policy Model for security policies, which specify what membership and connectivity a Fabric allows and which IP hosts may manage it. The other is FC-SP Zoning, a variant of Enhanced Zoning that keeps zoning management and enforcement independent from other policies.

Policies are held in Policy Objects: a Policy Summary Object (a list of pointers to the other active objects, each paired with a cryptographic hash), a Switch Membership List, a Node Membership List, an IP Management List, per-switch Switch Connectivity Objects and optional Attribute Objects. A Fabric has exactly one each of the first four active objects, and zero or more of the last two. To change policy, an administrator edits the non-active objects and then activates a new Policy Summary Object that references them.

Every Policy Object has a name stored as type, length and value. The RFC lists nine name types, including Node_Name, Port_Name, Wildcard, Alphanumeric Name and IPv4 and IPv6 Address Ranges.
sections.eli5: The Fabric keeps a set of rule sheets: who may join, who may connect to whom, and who may be the boss. You edit a draft copy, and when it is ready you switch the draft on in one go.

sections.title: Switch Roles and Policy Management
sections.content:
For a Fabric of n Switches and m Nodes, Switch Connectivity Objects could grow as O(n**2) for switch-to-switch links and O(n*m) for switch-to-node links. To scale, they are distributed only where needed, using three kinds of Switch. Server Switches keep all the Fabric-wide objects, all Switch Connectivity Objects and a full Zoning Database copy. Autonomous Switches keep the Fabric-wide objects, their own connectivity object and a full Zoning Database copy. Client Switches keep the Fabric-wide objects, their own connectivity object and only a subset of the Active Zone Set. If Client Switches are deployed, at least one Server Switch must be in the same Fabric.

Policy changes happen in a server session with a Security Policy Server. All writes occur inside a session, which begins with an SSB request (locking the Fabric through the EACA SW_ILS) and ends with an SSE request (releasing it through ERCA). Reads may happen at any time, but consistent data is guaranteed only inside a session. Active and non-active objects persist after a session ends.
sections.eli5: In a big building, not every guard needs the whole rulebook. Some keep the full book, and some only keep the pages about their own door and ask the head guard when they need more.

sections.title: The Five MIB Modules and Design Choices
sections.content:
The RFC defines five modules. T11-FC-SP-TC-MIB holds shared Textual Conventions and Object Identifiers for the cryptographic algorithms listed in FC-SP. T11-FC-SP-AUTHENTICATION-MIB has three tables (authentication entities, per-interface statistics, and recently rejected transactions) and two reject notifications. T11-FC-SP-ZONING-MIB extends the Zone Server MIB of RFC 4936 and adds notifications for success or failure when two Fabrics join. T11-FC-SP-POLICY-MIB covers active objects, activate and deactivate operations, non-active objects, statistics and notifications. T11-FC-SP-SA-MIB covers Security Association capabilities, proposals, traffic selectors, active SA pairs and an authentication-failure notification.

Several conventions recur. Fibre Channel management instances come from the FC-MGMT-MIB (RFC 4044). Fabric-related tables are indexed by a T11FabricIndex, which is always 1 for a device on a single physical Fabric without virtual Fabrics. Per-port data uses InterfaceIndexOrZero, where zero means one port or aggregated ports, and it is listed before the Fabric Index in an INDEX clause. Egress Traffic Selectors carry a unique precedence value and the numerically lowest one wins, while ingress frames on active SAs are checked against the selectors negotiated for the SPI in the frame. Certificates, CAs and CRLs are managed as in other networks, so no objects are defined for them.
sections.eli5: The standard is split into five binders, each covering one topic: shared words, who-is-who checks, clubs, rule sheets and secret-code links. Each binder lists its own dials and alarm bells.

sections.title: Notification Rate Control
sections.content:
Almost all notifications in these modules fire at the pace of operator actions, in the control plane. The exception is t11FcSpSaNotifyAuthFailure, which is driven by the data plane and could, in the worst case, occur for every received ingress frame.

So it is rate controlled. After the first authentication failure on a given Security Association, notifications for later failures are suppressed for the length of a time window, set by the read-write object t11FcSpSaControlWindow. Even the first failure's notification is suppressed once a configured number of SAs in a Fabric (t11FcSpSaControlMaxNotifs) have already sent one in the window. The failures themselves must still be detected and counted.
sections.eli5: If a burglar alarm rang for every single rattle of the door, you would go deaf. So it rings once, then stays quiet for a while, though the alarm still keeps count in secret.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC defines no MIB objects for the secrets used by DH-CHAP. Such secrets are highly sensitive and need to be strong, so they must be managed by other means. Each module then lists its writable objects (which in a non-secure environment could, for example, change the retained configuration, silence notifications, shorten or lengthen SA lifetimes, or shrink the audit trail of authentication rejects) and its readable objects (which could help an attacker study capabilities, policies or hashes).

The Policy module is the most sensitive, since editing non-active policies and then activating them could allow unauthorized switch or node connectivity, unauthorized management access, or weaker Security Associations. Because SNMP versions before SNMPv3 lack adequate security, the RFC says it is RECOMMENDED to consider SNMPv3 with cryptographic security, and deploying earlier versions is NOT RECOMMENDED. It also says implementations should consider denial-of-service risks from hash recomputation, with countermeasures such as requiring authentication for SETs and rate-limiting SET operations.
sections.eli5: The dials that change rules are powerful, so only trusted people should touch them. Use the strong lock (SNMPv3), not the old flimsy one.
